title: The Plug Door
passage:
Vault doors went round in the 1870s and stayed round for sixty years — not, as the guidebooks like to say, because a circle is the strongest shape. The reason was the seat. A square door has four corners, and a corner is where a crowbar or a charge of powder can find a gap to work in; a circular door was ground to a shallow taper and dropped into a matching taper in the frame, so that pressure from outside drove it further into its seat rather than opening one. Nor was it a question of mass: the plug doors of that period were often lighter than the slab doors they replaced. What finished them was a change of threat, since a drill cares nothing for corners, and by the 1940s the rectangular door was quietly back.
— Ivar Brandt, engineering historian

questions.prompt: According to the text, what made the round vault door hard to force?

options.text: Its weight: a plug door of that period was far heavier than the square door it replaced, and heavier than the tools of the day could shift.
Its tapered fit: force applied from outside pressed the door deeper into its seat instead of opening a gap at the rim.
Its curvature: the rounded face turned an explosive charge aside and spread the force around the frame rather than into the steel.
Its geometry: a shape without corners carries load evenly, so a round door could not be pulled out of true the way a square one could.

questions.rationale: TYPE-001 direct detail, keyed to the sentence that carries the passage's whole argument: the circular door 'was ground to a shallow taper and dropped into a matching taper in the frame, so that pressure from outside drove it further into its seat rather than opening one'. B paraphrases exactly that — the fit, not the shape, does the work. A = contradiction with a plausible outside intuition (heavy vault doors are the popular image, but the text states the opposite: 'the plug doors of that period were often lighter than the slab doors they replaced'). C = outside_knowledge with surface_word_match: the passage does mention 'a charge of powder', so explosives are in the reader's mind, but it uses them to explain why a corner is a weakness, and it never claims a curved face deflects or spreads a blast. D = the guidebook belief the writer opens by rejecting — 'not, as the guidebooks like to say, because a circle is the strongest shape' — and it is the most tempting distractor precisely because it is what most readers already believe about round doors.

generator_meta.topic: why bank vault doors were round for sixty years — the tapered plug seat rather than the strength of the circle, and why the shape was abandoned once drills replaced crowbars
